records.title: Record June 2025 marine heatwave covered 62% of the Mediterranean surface; 2025 was the second-warmest year on record
records.description: Copernicus Marine reported that June 2025 was the warmest June on record for the Mediterranean, with a mean sea surface temperature of 23.86 C, and that a high-intensity marine heatwave affected 62% of the sea surface at the peak. Its annual bulletin ranks 2025 as the second-warmest year, with the whole basin touched by a marine heatwave for the third year running.

location.detail: All Mediterranean coastal states; strongest in the western basin in June 2025

records.layer_rationale: Basin-scale sea-surface warming and marine heatwaves are a physical climate signal.

notes.harm: The Copernicus bulletin says marine heatwaves 'can have negative impact on the environment and ecosystems' but reports no specific ecological damage for 2025, so harm is potential only (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: None of the four cited sources reports a fishery, port or tourism restriction tied to the 2025 heatwave (refs 1-4).
notes.scale: Heatwave conditions covered up to 62% of the sea surface at the June 2025 peak and 93% of the basin reached strong or higher intensity during the year, a regional-sea extent (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The entire Mediterranean was affected by a marine heatwave at some point in 2025 for the third consecutive year, so the pattern is recurring (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The sources are monitoring bulletins and press releases with no advisory, closure or enforcement action, so no formal-notice credit is given (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: At the June 2025 peak, 62% of the Mediterranean Sea surface was affected by a high-intensity marine heatwave, up from 40% in the same period of 2024 (ref 1).

records.title: Mediterranean surface waters hit an all-time daily record of 28.47 C on 15 August 2024 in the warmest year then on record
records.description: Mercator Ocean, which runs the Copernicus Marine Service, reported that 15 August 2024 was the hottest day on record for Mediterranean surface waters, at a mean 28.47 C, and that surface temperatures had stayed above 28 C since 6 August. The 2025 Copernicus bulletin states that 99% of the basin saw strong or higher marine heatwaves in 2024, and a June 2025 report said the 28.47 C record still stood.

records.layer_rationale: Record basin-mean sea surface temperature is a physical climate signal.

notes.harm: Euronews, summarising Copernicus Climate Change Service data, says marine heatwaves cause coral bleaching and mass die-offs; this source reports no specific 2024 die-off count, so harm is limited here (ref 3).
notes.livelihoods: Euronews names disruption to fisheries, aquaculture and tourism as possible costs of marine heatwaves but gives no Mediterranean closure or loss figure (ref 3).
notes.scale: The record is a mean over the whole Mediterranean surface, 28.47 C on 15 August 2024, and 99% of the basin saw strong or higher marine heatwaves in 2024 (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Temperatures stayed above 28 C from 6 August, the longest such spell recorded, within a run of three consecutive years with basin-wide heatwaves (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Mercator note and the Euronews article are monitoring and press reports with no advisory, closure or enforcement action (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Greenpeace monitoring finds marine heatwaves down to 40 m and gorgonian and coral damage in Italian marine protected areas
records.description: Greenpeace Italia's Mare Caldo network reported repeated marine heatwaves at all 14 monitored Italian stations in 2025, including a 41-day heatwave at Asinara that reached 3.5 C above the climatological threshold, with heat reaching 30 to 40 m depth. Its earlier report found severe impact on 94% of Paramuricea clavata colonies at 25 m at Portofino, and necrosis or bleaching of gorgonians and the coral Cladocora caespitosa at several sites.

records.layer_rationale: Heat stress on habitat-forming gorgonians and corals is damage to benthic habitat.

notes.harm: At Portofino, 94% of Paramuricea clavata colonies at 25 m showed severe impact in the 2024 monitoring, and Elba lost colonies of Eunicella cavolini and P. clavata over six years (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.livelihoods: The Greenpeace reports and press coverage describe no fishery or diving closure at the monitored sites (refs 1-4).
notes.scale: Heatwaves were recorded at all 14 stations in 2025, 13 of them inside marine protected areas across Sardinia, Sicily, Liguria and Puglia, a national-coastline extent (ref 3).
notes.duration: The network recorded heatwaves in 2024 (14 at Asinara, 6 each at Portofino and Cinque Terre) and again in 2025, and links Elba's six-year decline to the 2023 and 2024 anomalies (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: The evidence is an NGO monitoring programme run with University of Genoa and OGS; no official notice or enforcement action is cited (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Venice's MOSE barrier raised 25 times in 2023 and 28 in 2024 as high tides hit a record; study warns it may fail by 2100 in the worst case
records.description: Venice's MOSE storm-surge barrier was raised 25 times in 2023 and 28 times in 2024, 97 times since 2020, while tides above 80 cm reached 219 events in 2024, the most recorded. A 2025 INGV study reported in Il Post found that in the highest-emissions scenario the 3 m sea-lagoon difference MOSE was designed for would be exceeded in 2100.

records.layer_rationale: Rising tides and subsidence drive coastal flood risk in the lagoon.

notes.harm: Tides of 80 cm or more rose to 219 events in 2024 including MOSE closures, with almost 800 hours above that level, so flood risk to the city is growing but the barrier is protecting it (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Port operators say each raising limits port operations and want more involvement in how MOSE is managed (ref 1).
notes.scale: The system protects one lagoon with three inlets; INGV maps flooding of about 139 km2 by 2150 around Lido, Cavallino, Chioggia and the airport (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: Tides above 80 cm rose from about 75 events a year around 2000 to 126 around 2020 and then to 219 in 2024, a chronic trend (ref 1).
notes.significance: No court ruling, order or emergency declaration is cited; MOSE operates under state management and critics call procedures provisional (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Cyclone Harry flooded the coasts of Calabria, Sicily and Sardinia in January 2026, with Sicily's initial damage put at 741.5 million euros

A study of Calabria's Ionian coast found peak total water levels of 3.47 to 5.03 m and impacts in 29 of 50 coastal municipalities, and Sicily's governor gave an initial damage estimate of 741.5 million euros.

records.title: Ebro Delta loses land to coastal retreat and subsidence as dams cut sediment, with state protection plan still pending in 2024
records.description: Spain's Ministry for the Ecological Transition says the Ebro Delta coast suffers erosion worsened by reduced sediment supply, subsidence averaging 3 mm a year, sea-level rise and more intense storms. NASA imagery shows a river-mouth island retreating by several hundred metres between 1984 and 2021, and in February 2024 a minister defended revising the coastal boundary while the State protection plan had not yet been presented.

notes.livelihoods: The 2022 sand reinforcement and farmers testing salt-tolerant rice show agriculture is under pressure, but no closure or displacement is reported (refs 3, 4).
notes.scale: The problem is one delta of about 320 km2 and a 50 km coast (ref 4).
notes.duration: Sediment transport downstream of the dams is estimated at 0.33 hm3 a year and the delta has been eroding for decades, with works in 2020, 2022 and 2024 (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: MITECO presented a formal Plan for the Protection of the Ebro Delta in November 2020 and a revision of the public maritime-terrestrial boundary was under way, a formal state process (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Nile Delta coast and Alexandria face erosion and rising seas as the World Bank projects annual flood losses up to 581 million dollars by 2050
records.description: Egypt's irrigation ministry says sea level rose up to 3.2 mm a year since 2012 while land under Alexandria and the delta sinks at a similar rate. A World Bank analysis reported in March 2022 estimates that a 0.3 m rise would flood about 30% of Alexandria and displace about 545,000 people, and that the delta coastline lost 78 hectares a year from 2001 to 2018.

notes.livelihoods: The World Bank figure of 504-581 million dollars of yearly Alexandria flood losses by 2050 and 70,500 job losses indicates economic disruption, not yet a closure (ref 2).
